metadata.title: GEEK Protocol — Toccata application design follow-up
metadata.schema: correctIndex is zero-based; options contains four distinct strings
metadata.reviewNotice: Internally source-checked original questions about the pinned Toccata guide revision, including experimental Argent and evolving vprogs designs. Not a current activation, deployment, audited-interface or universal-support claim. Difficulty is provisional. Advanced Toccata material remains outside the introductory Study topic filter.
metadata.attribution: GEEK Protocol original questions based on pinned Kaspanet documentation; source prose and code not imported.

questions.prompt: In the cited Toccata counter example, how does max_step differ from the count state field?
options: max_step is baked into the instance as a constructor constant; count encodes its current state
Both are mutable account-storage slots held by the node
count is a constructor-only constant while max_step is the changing state
Both values come from a mandatory market-price feed
questions.funFact: The guide distinguishes instance constants from state encoded in the redeem-script preimage. A transition changes the state commitment, not those constructor constants.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which distinction does the cited Toccata guide make between an auth group and a covenant group?
options: Auth groups contain all network UTXOs; covenant groups contain only fees
Auth groups find outputs authorized by one input; covenant groups find transaction members sharing an ID
Auth groups apply only to miners; covenant groups apply only to wallets
The two views always select exactly the same transaction subset
questions.funFact: Input-local output authorization and family-wide input/output membership answer different questions, especially in transactions carrying multiple flows.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How are Toccata covenant count/index opcode pairs used in the cited guide?
options: Assume every matching item has the same transaction index
Interpret the count as a token balance and the index as a signature
Ask the subset size, then obtain the transaction index of its k-th member
Read arbitrary historical UTXOs without a transaction context
questions.funFact: Count establishes the subset length; the corresponding index operation maps a member position to an actual input or output index.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: May a covenant transaction also carry ordinary fee/change items or another covenant flow in the cited Toccata design?
options: No; every input and output must belong to one covenant
Only if all covenant identifiers are deleted
Only if ordinary inputs bypass consensus validation
Yes; scripts identify and validate their relevant subsets
questions.funFact: The design allows several covenant flows plus ordinary funding and change in one transaction; the covenant script must locate its own relevant items.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why does forcing every update through one live state UTXO limit an application in the cited Toccata guide?
options: Each transition must spend and replace that same state UTXO in sequence
A single UTXO cannot have any spending script
Kaspa stops ordering unrelated transactions while it exists
Its existence disables all parallel blocks
questions.funFact: A singleton state machine is sequential. Applications with separable state can instead use multiple live UTXO lineages; a high block rate does not remove singleton contention.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How does the cited Toccata decision guide characterize miner-resolved covenant inputs that name a covenant ID rather than a specific UTXO?
options: The required standard transaction format for all new apps
A research path likely needing mempool and node support
A wallet-only setting that needs no protocol coordination
A production-stable Argent API required by consensus
questions.funFact: The guide presents miner-selected resolution of a covenant-bound input as research, not the normal first-app path. Matching signing rules and node/mempool support would need a concrete design.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why does a covenant-aware indexer need preimage or witness material in the cited Toccata state model?
options: A commitment contains an automatically readable JSON state object
Witness material supplies permission to ignore the covenant ID
A P2SH commitment alone does not decode the application state it commits to
A transaction ID always reveals every private application input
questions.funFact: Readers need the redeem-script preimage or enough witness data to interpret the committed state, alongside the live UTXO and provenance context.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What division of work does the cited Silverscript token example illustrate?
options: The macro decides token price while the policy selects the browser theme
The compiler replaces application invariants with miner discretion
The developer must hand-write every generated stack operation
The policy checks token conservation; the macro describes transaction layout and generates its wrapper
questions.funFact: Application policy and the surrounding covenant layout are distinct. The example policy equates input and output totals, while the declaration drives the generated transaction machinery.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What construction does the cited Silverscript guide use when validating state under a foreign contract template?
options: Expected template prefix, encoded state and template suffix
An arbitrary output label plus a matching token ticker
Only the successor transaction ID
Only the current account address and its balance
questions.funFact: Template-aware validation checks that the output encodes the proposed state under the expected contract template, using its prefix and suffix context.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which tool is identified as the compiler in the cited Silverscript workspace?
options: kaspad
silverc
kaspa-wallet
cli-debugger
questions.funFact: The guide lists silverc as the compiler and separately lists the source-level debugger and other compilation/ABI tooling.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which cited Silverscript tooling facility supports building the signature script for an entrypoint ABI?
options: OpChainblockSeqCommit
getVirtualChainFromBlock
build_sig_script
ComputeBudget::checked_covering_script_units
questions.funFact: build_sig_script handles entrypoint ABI support. The other named facilities concern sequencing, ingestion or execution-budget sizing.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which compilation direction does the cited experimental Argent guide describe?
options: Argent source to an Ethereum account-state database
Kaspa block headers to Java bytecode to Argent
Silverscript to a mandatory custodial wallet service
Argent source to generated Silverscript to Kaspa script
questions.funFact: Argent is presented as a higher source layer for covenant families. Its prototype lowers through Silverscript rather than adding a third execution architecture.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why must ordinary transitions preserve hidden template fields in the cited Argent design?
options: Later transitions need those fields to validate routes under the intended templates
They are temporary UI labels that never affect validation
They replace every business-state field in the app
They let any new output route become valid without checking
questions.funFact: Hidden ABI fields can carry route-safety context rather than business data. Losing or changing them can break validation of later successors.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How does the cited Argent route-commitment pattern keep long-lived state compact?
options: Store every possible route witness in each user account
Store a route root, then supply a route leaf, Merkle branch and template material when used
Replace route validation with a shared display name
Reconstruct the route root from a wallet password
questions.funFact: The pattern commits to routing data early and expands the particular route in a transition witness, which is checked against the stored root.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Can a shared covenant ID alone establish that one input is a Player actor and an output is a Game actor in the cited Argent model?
options: Yes; every shared covenant ID encodes all actor types
Yes; an actor role is determined only by the output position
No; template validation supplies the role identity within the family
No; actor roles are assigned solely by the explorer UI
questions.funFact: Family membership and actor role are different properties. A family ID survives state changes, while expected templates identify which roles participate.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What do consumes and emits describe in the cited Argent source model?
options: The native coin emission schedule and a mining hash rate
A wallet password and its recovery phrase
The number of proof workers and their memory limit
Peer actors consumed in the transaction and named authorized outputs
questions.funFact: These declarations express the participating peer inputs and authorized successor outputs, making family-level transition intent explicit before lowering.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Must each based-app user operation itself spend the settlement covenant in the cited Toccata model?
options: No; a user operation can be an ordinary v1 L1 transaction carrying lane and payload data
Yes; the settlement covenant must be consumed by every user operation
Yes; every user must own the settlement covenant private key
No; user operations exist only as unsigned messages kept off L1
questions.funFact: User operation submission and covenant settlement are separate paths: ordinary L1 operations are ordered first, and a later proof settles their execution.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Who supplies the meaning of a based-app operation payload in the cited Toccata guide?
options: Kaspa consensus by executing each app policy directly
The application runtime
The recipient address checksum
The block subsidy schedule
questions.funFact: L1 carries and orders the bytes; application-specific execution semantics belong to the runtime. Valid L1 inclusion does not by itself assert app-policy success.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What does the cited based-app settlement covenant track rather than directly executing every user operation?
options: The complete off-chain database as mutable node account storage
Only a user-selected app name with no state commitment
A compact commitment to application state, updated through settlement proofs
Every private witness as plaintext in a block header
questions.funFact: The settlement covenant checks a proven state transition and advances the compact app-state commitment; the runtime performs the application execution.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which boundary evidence brackets a lane-local transition proof in the cited based-app model?
options: Only a receipt from an unrelated wallet
A current token price before and after execution
Only a list of transactions that the executor chose to keep
App-lane inclusion at both a start anchor and an end anchor
questions.funFact: The proof model anchors lane inclusion at the beginning and end and proves the lane-local transition between those anchors.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why must a based-app proof bind to the sequencing commitment actually read by its settlement script in the cited guide?
options: A correct transition over unrelated L1 activity must not satisfy the settlement check
The commitment is only a UI label and should be ignored
The proof can choose any activity if its new state root is well formed
The commitment determines the wallet password used for signing
questions.funFact: The script-provided L1 anchor fixes the activity context. Proof validity without the intended activity binding would establish the wrong statement.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What does OpChainblockSeqCommit expose to a settlement script in the cited Toccata guide?
options: The current wallet seed phrase
The sequencing commitment of an eligible recent selected-parent-chain block
The complete plaintext application database
The Merkle root of an arbitrary unknown block chosen by the prover
questions.funFact: The referenced block must meet the guide’s visibility, age and compatibility conditions. The opcode provides an L1 sequencing anchor, not arbitrary historical access.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How does the cited vprogs runtime pattern relate execution to later proof production?
options: Every user operation waits for its final L1 aggregate proof before any execution
Proof workers replace the execution stage entirely
Execution can commit app state while proof workers build later settlement artifacts
Executing an operation automatically proves final settlement
questions.funFact: The described pipeline separates execution progress from receipt, batch, aggregate and settlement work. Execution progress is not a claim that settlement already occurred.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How does the cited evolving vprogs pattern represent an L1 chain block containing no app operations?
options: It silently removes the block from the processing sequence
It invents a no-fee user transfer to fill the batch
It resets the app state to genesis
It still creates an empty batch for that chain block
questions.funFact: The documented pattern creates a batch for every L1 chain block, including empty ones. This is a scoped runtime design, not a promise about every implementation version.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which receipt-composition order does the cited vprogs guide describe?
options: Transaction receipts into batch receipts, then batch receipts into aggregates
Aggregate receipts into wallet mnemonics, then into transactions
Block headers into token tickers, then into account passwords
One independent final settlement proof per opcode with no batching
questions.funFact: The pipeline composes smaller execution receipts into batches and larger aggregates before producing settlement material.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Besides state and lane commitments, which program identities appear in the cited vprogs StateTransition journal?
options: The user’s browser-extension name and theme
Transaction-processor and batch-processor guest image IDs
The explorer operator’s username and email
Only the transaction’s recipient nickname
questions.funFact: The journal includes tx_image_id and batch_image_id, binding the settlement statement to its processing programs as well as its state/activity context.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which question does the cited Toccata decision guide prioritize when choosing an application architecture?
options: Does the application have the largest possible feature list?
Can every user choose a different native coin supply?
Can state be partitioned into parallel UTXOs, or does shared mutable state dominate?
Does the website use a particular front-end framework?
questions.funFact: The guide treats state layout as the useful starting point. Its choices are design heuristics rather than automatic guarantees of performance or suitability.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What design burden does the cited Toccata guide assign to replicated shared-state UTXOs?
options: Assume consensus automatically merges all replica updates
Remove all indexer evidence because replicas cannot disagree
Guarantee every replica is always current without propagation
Define tolerated staleness, conflict resolution and safety during temporary divergence
questions.funFact: Replication moves obligations into application protocol design, including what users and indexers can establish while replicas diverge.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which proof-system tag mapping is described in the cited Toccata Inline ZK guide?
options: 0x20 for Groth16 and 0x21 for RISC Zero Succinct
0x20 for Schnorr and 0x21 for ECDSA
0x20 for RISC Zero Succinct and 0x21 for Groth16
Both tags identify an unpriced arbitrary program interpreter
questions.funFact: The precompile dispatches to the named proof verifier by tag. That tag must be interpreted under the cited revision’s verification rules.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which limitation does the cited Toccata guide explicitly attach to its compact BN254 Groth16 proof mode?
options: It cannot be verified by a script
It is not post-quantum
It contains no verification key or public-input context
It gives automatic access to every private application witness
questions.funFact: The guide distinguishes the compact Groth16 mode from the larger STARK-based RISC Zero Succinct mode. A proof-mode label should not be expanded into unsupported security guarantees.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: In the cited Inline ZK model, how can L1 represent state while detailed transition data remains private?
options: Put every private witness in a plaintext block header
Hide the existence of all transactions from consensus
Keep state commitments on L1 and use a proof computed from private witness data
Remove the successor-state commitment from the covenant
questions.funFact: The diagram separates private state/witness data from public commitments. Privacy does not mean the chain has no visible state commitments or transaction activity.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What does the gas field represent in the cited Toccata based-app operation table?
options: The app’s final accepted state root
A plaintext copy of the private proving witness
A per-wallet native-coin balance
A lane gas commitment
questions.funFact: The operation table assigns gas to the lane gas commitment. Payload interpretation belongs to the app runtime, and a gas value is not itself an execution-result or settlement proof.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How does the cited Toccata pricing table make Groth16 verification cost depend on public inputs?
options: A fixed base plus 250,000 script units multiplied by (public-input count + 1)
A flat one-script-unit cost regardless of input count
Only the byte length of the transaction’s recipient address
A subtraction of 250,000 units for every extra public input
questions.funFact: The cited formula is 14,000,000 + 250,000 × (public inputs + 1) script units, following the gamma_abc element count.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: How many committed script units does one v1 compute-budget unit buy in the cited Toccata pricing ladder, before the separate free allowance?
options: 100 script units
10,000 script units
1,000 script units
100,000 script units
questions.funFact: The guide converts one compute-budget unit into 100 compute grams and each gram into 100 script units. The free per-input allowance is separate.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why does the cited Toccata guide recommend estimating a tight valid compute budget instead of setting it unnecessarily high?
options: A higher budget permanently changes the application’s token supply
An excessive budget disables every spending rule
An excessive budget raises mass and fees and worsens block admission
A lower declared budget is always valid regardless of runtime work
questions.funFact: Budget sizing has costs as well as a validation floor. Builders should estimate the actual generated script and proof path.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What is the charging unit for signature verification in the cited Toccata pricing guide?
options: Only a whole transaction that ultimately succeeds
Only the first valid signature in an entire block
Only the number of characters in an account name
Each cryptographic verification attempt, including attempts inside multisig-style opcodes
questions.funFact: The guide assigns 100,000 script units per verification attempt, so a multisig-style path is not priced solely by whether its final result succeeds.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which extra script-public-key size cost appears in the cited Toccata pricing table?
options: 100 script units per spent-UTXO script-public-key byte beyond 35 bytes
One sompi for each character in the recipient nickname
No charge for script-public-key bytes of any size
100 script units for every unspent output on the network
questions.funFact: This pricing event concerns the spent UTXO’s script public key above the standard 35-byte size, not every network output or a displayed address string.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Which stack event is charged at one script unit per byte in the cited Toccata pricing table?
options: Every byte in the node’s entire historical database
Bytes newly pushed into execution stacks
The number of output addresses shown by an explorer
The decimal digits in the current KAS market price
questions.funFact: The runtime meter charges newly pushed execution-stack bytes, alongside other events such as hashing and proof/signature verification.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: What does the cited ComputeBudget::checked_covering_script_units helper return when the covering budget cannot fit the v1 u16 field?
options: A wrapped smaller budget
A negative budget
None
An automatically valid unlimited budget
questions.funFact: The helper accounts for the free allowance and rounds upward, but explicitly reports an unrepresentable result instead of wrapping it into a smaller field.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.

questions.prompt: Why can a relayer adjust compute_budget without invalidating v1 signatures in the cited Toccata design?
options: V1 signatures never commit to any transaction data
The relayer automatically receives every signer’s private key
The budget is copied into a wallet UI field and never used in validation
The budget is outside the signed intent, while the block-level transaction hash still commits to it
questions.funFact: The guide separates resource fitting from signed user policy. Adjustability does not remove runtime budget validation or the block’s commitment to the chosen resource value.
questions.attribution: GEEK Protocol original question based on the cited Kaspanet documentation revision; no source prose or code imported.
